definition: Lacking flavor, or so dull and bland that it fails to hold anyone's interest.
example: The sequel's insipid dialogue made even the talented cast seem bored with their own lines.
nuance: Insipid stresses a lack of flavor or spark and fits both food and ideas, while vapid stresses emptiness of thought.
prompt: A food critic tastes the soup at a newly opened restaurant.
options: The critic found the soup insipid, with barely a trace of salt or herbs.
The critic called the soup insipid because its fiery peppers made her eyes water for minutes.
An insipid draft from the kitchen door slowly chilled the dining room without anyone noticing.
The insipid restaurant had opened its doors for the very first time only three days earlier.
reasons: A soup with almost no seasoning is flat and tasteless, so the word fits.
A fiercely spicy soup has strong flavor, which is the reverse of blandness.
This confuses the word with insidious, which describes harm that creeps in unnoticed.
Being new or just beginning is incipient, a look-alike word, not a lack of flavor.

practice.prompt: A teacher gives feedback on a student's draft of a class speech.
options: Her teacher said the speech felt insipid, full of safe clichés and lacking any personal story.
The speech was so insipid that the audience leaped to their feet cheering after every line.
The insipid speaker bravely volunteered to go first despite her fear of crowds.
Insipid nerves about speaking grew quietly worse each week until he dreaded class.
reasons: Stale phrases and no personal spark make a speech dull, which is exactly the point.
Wild enthusiasm from listeners suggests a lively speech, not a lifeless one.
Courage is described by intrepid, a look-alike; the word here means dull, not brave.
Gradually worsening harm is insidious; the word in question concerns blandness.
